dialog.body: Public Works, good morning, this is Denise.
Morning. Sorry, can I get your last name too? I keep a log of every call on this.
Sure, Arruda. A-R-R-U-D-A.
Arruda. Okay. Denise, I think I actually talked to you Monday night. Diogo Resendes, 14 Wellington Avenue, Fifth Ward. My parents' house. The storm drain at the corner.
Oh, yes, I remember. You called right around dinnertime. Hang on, let me pull it up. [pause] Okay, I've got it. Repeat backup, and a crew went out yesterday.

Right. So the crew came yesterday, around lunchtime. They ran the hose thing down the line, the jetter. And the guy told my father it was partly blocked. Partly. Which, okay, great, now we know. But that's two storms this winter that drain backed up and our basement flooded, and I'm sitting here looking at the forecast and I have no idea if they actually got it all.
Okay.

Because, see, I have it written down. The first time was the January coastal storm, overnight Friday into Saturday the tenth. Six inches in the basement. My father called on the twelfth, somebody came on the fourteenth, and all they did was clean off the grate and shovel the sand out around the top. That's it. Then Sunday into Monday, the snow-to-rain storm, it floods again. Four inches this time. Second time this winter. And the basement's finished, it's carpet down there, my parents' rec room, the washer and dryer. We're still pulling stuff out.
I hear you. That's two in about two weeks, that's a lot.

And it's not like we just sat there. After the first one I went and got sandbags, put them all along the front by the door. Did nothing. Water came in anyway. So whatever's going on, it's not something we can fix from our side. It's the drain.
Okay. So what I'm seeing here, yesterday's note says they jetted the line under the corner and found a partial blockage. It doesn't say whether they think it's fully clear now.

See, that's my problem. Partly blocked, and then what? Did they clear it? Is there something broken down there? Nobody said. They talked to my father for like two minutes, and he's seventy-seven, he's not going to ask the follow-up questions. So what I'm asking, I want somebody to go back out there and check it. Today, if you can. Look at it properly and clear it, all the way, before anything else comes through.
I can put in a request to have the crew go back and check that line, and I'll mark it urgent with the history. Today I can't promise, they've still got a list from the storm, but it goes in now.
Okay. Hold on, I'm writing. Request to recheck the line, marked urgent. [pause] Okay. And on Monday you told me a supervisor would call by Thursday. It's Thursday. Nobody's called.
It's still on here for today. Day's not over, but I'll send it up again so it doesn't sit.

I appreciate that, I do. It's just, every time it's the same thing. We call, somebody comes, they do a little bit, and then it rains again. My mother, I mean my father's husband, Paulo, he's down there with a wet vac at two in the morning. They're in their seventies. This can't keep happening.
No, I get it. Let me ask you, is it the same corner each time? Wellington, the catch basin at the corner by the house?
Same corner, same basin. The street ponds up right in front and it just sits. And there's something else I wanted to ask. Is there a permanent fix? Because jetting it once a month isn't a plan.

That's a fair question, and it's not one I can answer from here. What I can do is flag the address for engineering. With two floods and two crew visits, it should get looked at for something bigger. The supervisor can tell you more when he calls.

Flagged for engineering. Okay. [pause] And can you put us on some kind of list? Like before the next storm, somebody calls us, or comes and checks that basin ahead of time? I don't want to find out the drain's blocked when there's already water in the basement.
I'll add a note asking for a call before the next storm, with your number as the contact. Is that still your cell, ending in one eight six?
Yes. 401-555-0186. That's me, not the house. Call me, not my parents.

Got it, you're the contact. So, recap: recheck of the line at the corner, marked urgent. Supervisor callback, sent up again for today. Flagged for engineering for a longer-term fix. And a pre-storm callback request to you.

Recheck, supervisor, engineering, pre-storm call. Okay. I've got all four. [pause] Sorry, I'm also standing out front right now looking at the basin and the new people across the street put up this flag, I swear I've never seen it in my life. Green and white with some kind of bird. I've been trying to figure it out all week. Anyway. Doesn't matter.
I couldn't tell you either. Is the basin itself clear right now? Anything sitting on the grate?
Grate's clear. Some leftover snowbank next to it but the top's open. That was never the problem, though. The problem's down in the line.
Understood. I'm putting that in the notes too, that the grate's clear and the concern is the line, so they don't just look at the top and leave again.
Yeah. Please. Because that's exactly what happened the first time. They looked at the top and left.
It's in there. And if you don't hear from the supervisor by end of day, call back and ask for me, I'll chase it.
I will. Denise Arruda, Thursday, nine-thirty. Okay. Thanks. I just want this to be the last time I'm calling about it.
I hope so too. Take care, Diogo.
